explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The text says no one claimed that any of his possessions was his own, “but they shared everything they owned.” A whole crowd where nobody says "mine" is a miracle on its own. I can't set a plate of cookies down without somebody calling dibs.

explanations.answer: They give it all to the priests
explanations.explanation: Priests don't show up in this part of the story at all. The text says the believers shared everything they owned. When money comes in, it's laid at the apostles' feet and then given out to people who have need. So the stuff keeps moving through the community instead of piling up in one place.

explanations.answer: They store it all in the temple
explanations.explanation: Nothing gets stored in this story, friend. The believers shared everything they owned, and the money was given out to anyone who had need. A pile of stuff nobody touches sounds like the junk drawer I lived in for years. This crowd keeps everything moving.

That's it, baker. The money was laid at the apostles' feet "for distribution to anyone as he had need." The apostles aren't keeping it. They're a stop on the way to whoever needs it. I think that's how a good cookie box works too, because it's meant to be passed along.

The apostles are where the money gets laid, but they aren't where it ends up. The text says it was for distribution to anyone as he had need. So the apostles hand it out. They don't pocket it. Think of them as the folks passing the plate along.
The text doesn't narrow it down to widows. It says the money was distributed to anyone as he had need. That's a wide-open door, friend. Whoever has the need gets helped.

Not quite, baker. The text says the opposite: "There were no needy ones among them." People who owned lands or houses would sell their property and bring the proceeds to the apostles. That's how nobody was left going without. Everybody's need got covered.

Right, it's false. The text says there were no needy ones among them. The reason it gives is that those who owned lands or houses would sell their property and bring the proceeds. So the need got met, and nobody was left empty-handed. Not one person.

You got it, baker. Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus, is called Barnabas by the apostles, and the text says that means Son of Encouragement. That's a nickname you'd want on your apron. I've been called worse, and mostly by the dust in a junk drawer.

Thunder is a loud name, friend, but it isn't this one. The text says Barnabas means Son of Encouragement. Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus, gets that name from the apostles. Encouragement is a much better fit for a man who sells a field to help others.

Peace is a lovely name, but it's not the one here. The text says Barnabas means Son of Encouragement. The apostles gave that name to Joseph, a Levite from Cyprus. It tells you a lot about the kind of man he was.
That's right, baker. Barnabas sold a field he owned, brought the money and laid it at the apostles' feet. He did it with no fuss. Remember this one, because the very next story leans on it.

It's true, friend. The text says Barnabas sold a field he owned, brought the money, and laid it at the apostles' feet. That's exactly what the other believers were doing. He's the example the story hands us right before the next scene.

explanations.answer: Keeps back some and brings the rest
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says, baker. Ananias kept back some of the proceeds for himself, but brought a portion and laid it at the apostles' feet. He sold the property, but he didn't bring all of it. It's the story's turning point.

explanations.answer: Brings every bit of it to the apostles
explanations.explanation: Close to Barnabas, but not this man. The text says Ananias kept back some of the proceeds for himself. He brought only a portion to the apostles. That's what sets this scene apart from the last one.

explanations.answer: Gives all of it to his neighbors
explanations.explanation: The neighbors don't come up in this story, friend. Ananias kept back some of the money for himself and brought a portion to the apostles' feet. Nothing in the text sends the money to the folks next door. The question is about what he held onto.
The text says otherwise, baker. Ananias kept back some of the proceeds "with his wife's full knowledge." So Sapphira knew exactly what he was doing. This wasn't a one-person decision.
Right, it's false. The text says Ananias kept back some of the proceeds with his wife's full knowledge. Sapphira, his wife, knew what he was keeping. Later Peter says she agreed to it too (Acts 5:9).

You got it, baker. Peter, one of the apostles, asks how Satan has filled Ananias's heart "to lie to the Holy Spirit." Then he says, "You have not lied to men, but to God!" That tells you who was really on the receiving end of this lie.
No elders are named in this scene, friend. Peter, one of the apostles, says Ananias lied "to the Holy Spirit." And he adds that it wasn't to men but to God. The elders never come into it.

The high priest isn't in this scene at all. Peter, one of the apostles, says Satan filled Ananias's heart to lie to the Holy Spirit. He goes on to say it wasn't men Ananias lied to, but God. So the answer is the Holy Spirit.

Peter never says that, baker. He asks, "Did it not belong to you before it was sold? And after it was sold, was it not at your disposal?" So the land and the money were Ananias's own to decide about. The problem Peter names is the lie.

That's right, it's false. Peter asks Ananias, "Did it not belong to you before it was sold? And after it was sold, was it not at your disposal?" Nobody was making Ananias hand over every coin. Peter's complaint is that he lied about it.
That's what the text says, baker. On hearing these words, Ananias fell down and died. This is a heavy part of the story. I think it's one to read slowly.
No running here, friend. The text says that on hearing these words, Ananias fell down and died. It's a heavy moment, and I think it's best to just let it be heavy.

explanations.answer: He goes to get the rest
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't have Ananias going anywhere. On hearing Peter's words, he fell down and died. It's a heavy part of the story, and nobody in it gets a chance to fix things.
You got it, baker. The text says great fear came over all who heard what had happened. People couldn't brush this one off. It stuck with them.
Joy isn't what the text says here, friend. It says great fear came over all who heard what had happened. This was a serious moment, and the people in it knew it.
Anger isn't the word in the text. It says great fear came over all who heard what had happened. The people who heard it were shaken.
That's right, baker. About three hours later Sapphira came in, "unaware of what had happened." The young men had already buried Ananias. She walks in knowing none of it.
It's true, friend. The text says Sapphira came in about three hours later, unaware of what had happened. She hadn't heard a word about her husband. She walked into that room with no idea.

That's what she says, baker. Peter asks, "is this the price you and your husband got for the land?" and Sapphira answers yes, that is the price. She gives the same story Ananias did. It's the answer that leads to Peter's next words.

explanations.answer: No we kept some of it
explanations.explanation: That isn't what Sapphira says, friend. Peter asks whether this is the price she and her husband got for the land, and she answers yes, that is the price. She doesn't own up to anything. Her answer is what Peter responds to next.

explanations.answer: I would have to ask him
explanations.explanation: Sapphira doesn't ask anybody, baker. When Peter asks if this is the price she and her husband got for the land, she answers right away. She says yes, that is the price. No stalling, and no checking with anyone.
You got it, baker. Peter says, "How could you agree to test the Spirit of the Lord?" He says "agree" because Sapphira had gone along with it. Her answer to him is what Peter is speaking to.
Honor is the opposite of what Peter says, friend. His words are, "How could you agree to test the Spirit of the Lord?" The word he uses is test. That's how he describes what Sapphira agreed to do.
Follow isn't the word, baker. Peter asks, "How could you agree to test the Spirit of the Lord?" The word is test. He's asking how she could agree to that.

That's what the text says, baker. The young men came in and, finding her dead, carried her out and buried her beside her husband. It's a quiet, heavy ending for the two of them. The story doesn't add anything more to that moment.
The text doesn't mention a city gate, friend. It says the young men carried her out and buried her beside her husband. That's the detail it gives us. Nothing else is added.

The text doesn't send her back to the land, baker. The young men carried her out and buried her beside her husband. The land is the property they had sold, but it's not where the story puts her. She's laid next to Ananias.
